food.text: Before 1990, East German cuisine was shaped by other nations of the Communist bloc. East Germans holidayed in those countries, and soldiers stationed in East Germany brought their own dishes with them. Russian Soljanka entered the East German kitchen this way.

Balkan Grills have been present in West Germany since the 1960s, popularizing ćevapčići in the country. Restaurants serving Balkan food were often called Yugoslavian until the outbreak of the Yugoslav Wars. Those that survive are often now called Croatian instead.

Even today, the majority of Germany's coffee and tea imports are managed by the port of Hamburg. The varieties are mixed there, and coffee beans are roasted there. They are then distributed throughout Germany and other parts of continental Europe.

Until the 20th century, Hamburg's cuisine was defined by a wide choice of fish from the river Elbe and the Baltic Sea. Vierlande supplied fresh vegetables, Altes Land supplied fruit, and Wilhelmsburg was the city's 'milk isle' until industrialization.

Hamburg's cuisine has lost some of its distinct character because of the supraregional harmonization of North German cuisine. Even so, its high economic importance means it has many internationally recognized gourmet restaurants. Eleven of them were awarded a Michelin star in 2010.

Until the middle of the 20th century, the predominant schnapps in Hamburg were Köm, the northern German version of Aquavit, and Korn, distilled from rye or wheat. The small island of Neuwerk, which belongs to Hamburg, is famous for producing its own Aquavit.
In Saxony-Anhalt, rye is grown near Borde and used to make Burger Knäckebrot, a flatbread produced there since 1931. Cereal grains occupy 62% of the region's cultivated land.

art.text: The Bauhaus was founded by Walter Gropius in 1919 and became the most influential art and architecture school of the 20th century. Although it had no architecture department at first, Gropius saw in architecture the "ultimate goal of all artistic activity."

In 1937 the Nazis held a Degenerate Art exhibition in Munich, showing 650 modernist artworks taken from museums, poorly hung alongside graffiti and text labels mocking the art and the artists. Slogans painted on the walls included "Revelation of the Jewish racial soul," "An insult to German womanhood" and "The ideal—cretin and whore." The show was designed to inflame public opinion against modernism and to promote the idea that it was a conspiracy by people who hated German decency, frequently identified as Jewish-Bolshevist, although only 6 of the 112 artists included were in fact Jewish. It then traveled to several other cities in Germany and Austria.

Under the Nazis, art was meant to follow classical Greek and Roman models, which Hitler saw as embodying an inner racial ideal. It was also to be comprehensible to the average man, and both heroic and romantic. Between 1933 and 1945 the regime both promoted and censored forms of art.

Under the Weimar government of the 1920s, Germany emerged as a leading center of the avant-garde. It was the birthplace of Expressionism in painting and sculpture, and of the atonal music of Arnold Schoenberg. It also produced the jazz-influenced work of Paul Hindemith and Kurt Weill.

The Bauhaus in Weimar was shut down in 1925, a year after nationalist parties gained a majority in the Thuringian state parliament. That same year Gropius began building a new school in Dessau, completed in 1926. The Bauhaus Dessau is by far the most famous monument of classical modern art in Germany.

The Novembergruppe was founded on 3 December 1918, and around 100 avant-garde artists joined it. It held 19 exhibitions in Berlin before the Nazi regime banned it in 1933. Its shows in Rome, Moscow and Japan brought the German avant-garde to world attention.

Erich Mendelsohn's Einstein Tower in Potsdam is the major permanent extant landmark of Expressionist architecture. Many other important Expressionist works stayed on paper because economic conditions limited built commissions between 1914 and the mid-1920s. Examples include Bruno Taut's Alpine Architecture and Hermann Finsterlin's Formspiels.

The Novembergruppe was founded on 3 December 1918, in the aftermath of the November beginning of the German Revolution, when communists, anarchists and pro-republic supporters fought in the streets for control of the government. Around 100 avant-garde artists of many genres joined it. It held 19 exhibitions in Berlin and showed work in Rome, Moscow and Japan, until the Nazi regime banned it in 1933.

In 1933 and 1934 some Nazis were confused about Expressionism. Goebbels believed the forceful works of Emil Nolde, Ernst Barlach and Erich Heckel exemplified the Nordic spirit, but a faction led by Rosenberg despised Expressionism. The dispute ended in September 1934, when Hitler declared there would be no place for modernist experimentation in the Reich.

The Nazis planned a Führermuseum in Linz to display plundered art that Hitler considered good. It was never created. A stockpile of over 12000 pieces of stolen art at the Altaussee salt mines was reportedly slated for destruction with eight 500-kilogram bombs.
art.source_title: Art theft and looting during World War II

art.text: The Zeche Zollverein in Essen was built from 1927 to 1932 by Fritz Schupp and Martin Kremmer. It is counted among the most important buildings of the modernist period in Germany. It stands alongside Berlin's Horseshoe housing estate of 1930 by Bruno Taut and Martin Wagner.

On 6 November 1945, art protection officer Walter Farmer prevented the US from taking 202 valuable pictures from German collections, an effort called operation "Westward Ho". He assembled 24 colleagues from Germany and Austria to do it. Before his death in 1997, Farmer received Germany's Commander's Cross of the Order of Merit.
art.source_title: Art theft and looting during World War II

art.text: Rudolf Steiner designed a second Goetheanum after the first was destroyed by fire in 1922. Work began in 1924 and was completed in 1928.

war.text: Nazi Germany invaded Poland and captured the Free City of Danzig on 1 September 1939, beginning World War II in Europe. Poland fell quickly, and by the end of 1939 some 65,000 Polish intelligentsia, noblemen, clergy, and teachers had been murdered, using lists prepared in advance, in an attempt to destroy Poland's identity as a nation. Allied with Fascist Italy and other Axis powers, Germany had conquered most of Europe by 1940 but failed to subdue Britain.

Of the estimated 70 to 85 million deaths attributed to World War II, around 30 million occurred on the Eastern Front, including 9 million children. Nazi Germany waged a war of annihilation there, marked by brutality, scorched earth tactics, mass deportations, starvation, wholesale terrorism and massacres, including the genocidal Generalplan Ost and Hunger Plan, which sought the extermination and ethnic cleansing of more than a hundred million Eastern Europeans. Historian Geoffrey Roberts noted that more than 80 percent of all combat during the war took place there.

Between 1944 and 1950, some 12 to 14 million German-speaking refugees and expellees arrived in Western and central Germany from the former eastern territories and other countries in Eastern Europe; an estimated two million of them died on the way there. Many of the ethnic Germans, primarily women and children and especially those under Polish and Czechoslovak authorities, were severely mistreated before being deported. Thousands died in forced labor camps such as Lambinowice, Zgoda, Potulice and Jaworzno, while others starved, died of disease, or froze to death in slow, ill-equipped trains or in transit camps.

The German 8.8 cm Flak, called "acht und acht", was an unsurpassed achievement of artillery technology, with a muzzle velocity of 1000 m/s. In summer 1944 the Wehrmacht had 40,000 of these guns, and in October 1944 alone they fired 3.1 million shells.
war.source_title: Science and technology in Nazi Germany

war.text: Hitler seized Austria in the Anschluss of 1938, then took the Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia. Germany later signed a non-aggression pact with the Soviet Union and invaded Poland in 1939.

Rüdiger Overmans concluded that total German military deaths in World War II were 5.3 million, much higher than the German High Command had reported. This included 900,000 men conscripted from outside Germany's 1937 borders, in Austria and in east-central Europe. Of about 2 million listed as missing and presumed dead, Overmans believes 700,000 died in Soviet custody without being reported as POWs, and he estimates about 1.1 million German POWs died in captivity in all. In 1945 alone, he says, about 300,000 soldiers a month, some 10,000 men a day, died.
war.source_title: German casualties in World War II

war.text: In March 1935, Hitler announced the creation of an air force and said the Reichswehr would be increased to 550,000 men. Three months later, Britain agreed to German naval expansion in the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935.

The Soviet Union invaded Poland on 17 September 1939, 16 days after Nazi Germany invaded from the West. Britain and France never declared war on the Soviets, because Lord Halifax said Britain's obligation under the Anglo-Polish Agreement was restricted to Germany.
war.source_title: British declaration of war on Germany (1939)

war.text: Estimates of German civilians killed by Allied strategic bombing alone range from around 350,000 to 500,000; the West German government in 1956 gave 635,000 air raid dead including refugees in the east. Richard Overy estimated that about 25,000 were killed in Dresden, less than half the 60,000 in the official German figures, and reached an overall figure of 353,000 air war deaths. The US Strategic Bombing Survey noted that about 25% of known deaths in 1944 and 1945 were still unrecovered and unrecorded.
war.source_title: German casualties in World War II

war.text: On 7 December 1970, during a visit to Warsaw, Chancellor Willy Brandt knelt before a monument to those killed in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. It was a gesture of humility and penance that no German chancellor had made until then. Brandt won the Nobel Peace Prize for 1971.

The death rate of prisoners of war in World War II was higher than in World War I, which Christian Gerlach explained by "much higher prisoner numbers, more supply problems, politically motivated denial of food, hard labor and direct violence", including racism. About 14%, roughly 5 million POWs, died in captivity, about 3 million of them Soviets held by Germany and about one million Germans. The last POWs of World War II were Germans and Japanese released from Soviet camps in 1956.
war.source_title: Prisoners of war in World War II

war.text: András Toma is considered the last prisoner of war of World War II to be released. He was discovered living in a Russian psychiatric hospital in 2000 and was returned to Hungary some fifty-six years after his capture.
war.source_title: Prisoners of war in World War II

literature.text: East German literature was produced from 1945 until the end of communist government in 1990. It was heavily influenced by socialist realism and controlled by the government, and for decades it was dismissed as "Boy meet Tractor literature". Its study is now considered a legitimate field.

German language authors have won the Nobel Prize in Literature fourteen times as of 2023, the third most of any language. Only French authors (16 laureates) and English authors (32) have won more. German-language winners include Thomas Mann, Hermann Hesse, Günter Grass and Peter Handke.

Franz Kafka is widely regarded as a major figure of 20th-century literature. His work is interpreted as exploring alienation, existential anxiety, guilt and absurdity. His best-known works include the novella The Metamorphosis (1915) and the novels The Trial (1924) and The Castle (1926).

Under the Nazi regime, some German-language authors went into exile, producing what is called Exilliteratur. Others stayed and submitted to censorship, a stance known as "internal emigration", or Innere Emigration.

Post-war literature of West Germany, from 1945 to 1967, included Heinrich Böll, Günter Grass, Group 47 and Trümmerliteratur. Holocaust literature by writers such as Paul Celan and Edgar Hilsenrath also belongs to this period.
Thea von Harbou wrote the science fiction novels Metropolis (1925) and The Rocket to the Moon (1928). Both were adapted into silent films directed by Fritz Lang.

From 1949, the two opposing Germanys shaped science fiction on both sides of the Iron Curtain. In West Germany, the American space opera model gave rise to a successful series called Perry Rhodan. In East Germany, the socialist regime strictly controlled the genre, banned even the term "Science Fiction" as evoking anti-humanist and imperialist literature, and censored American production, so that the only legitimate purpose left for anticipation literature was utopia.
The literature of the 1950s in East Germany is known as Aufbau, meaning 'building up'. It was concerned with the establishment of industry and raised the ordinary worker to the status of hero.
Christa Wolf's Divided Sky (Der geteilte Himmel, 1963) and The Quest for Christa T. (Nachdenken über Christa T., 1968) are among the works listed under East German literature.

Much East German literature was anti-fascist. It was written by exiles who had escaped Nazi Germany and returned to the Soviet Occupation Zone. Their typical biography included defending the Weimar Republic, then exile, then supporting an antifascist-democratic reform through their writing.

The critic Georg Lukács greatly influenced East German literature. He rejected authors including Willi Bredel, James Joyce, Franz Kafka and Ernst Ottwalt over how their characters developed. He held up Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Lehrjahre as the model authors should emulate.

The first German science fiction magazine appeared in 1955 as Utopia-Sonderband. It was renamed Utopia Science Fiction Magazin between 1956 and 1957, then Utopia Magazin, and ended with its twenty-sixth issue in 1959.

Galaxis, launched in 1958, was the German edition of the American magazine Galaxy and printed almost only translated short stories. Its editor, Lothar Heinecke, frequently retouched and simplified the original texts.

science.text: In 1938, Otto Hahn discovered nuclear fission together with the Austrian scientist Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann. The discovery was the scientific and technological basis for the utilization of atomic energy. Hahn was also a pioneer of radioactivity and radiochemistry.

After World War II, Germany, German science and German as the language of science all lost their leading position. Many researchers' and teachers' careers had been ended by Nazi Germany, which started a brain drain, by denazification, by the American Operation Paperclip and the Soviet Operation Osoaviakhim, which exacerbated the brain drain, or simply by losing the war.

Generous Nazi Party funding and an abundance of world class technical institutions produced innovations still used today. They included rocketry, more protective helmets for soldiers, gasoline canisters, radio communication, and even Fanta soda.
science.source_title: Science and technology in Nazi Germany

science.text: Nazi Germany's first nuclear effort began in April 1939, months after fission was discovered in Berlin in December 1938. It ended before the September 1939 invasion of Poland, when many physicists were drafted into the Wehrmacht. A second effort under the Heereswaffenamt began on September 1, 1939.
science.source_title: German nuclear program during World War II

science.text: On May 1, 1934, Bernhard Rust was appointed Reich Minister of Science, Education and Culture. He was charged with leading science in the spirit of party ideology and preparing for war.
science.source_title: Science and technology in Nazi Germany

science.text: The German Academy of Sciences at Berlin was reopened in 1946 in the Eastern Sector by the Russian military government. It was renamed the Academy of Sciences of the GDR in 1972 and became East Germany's most eminent research institution. Its learned society was dissolved in 1992.
science.source_title: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin
tags: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin

science.text: The German nuclear program grew into three efforts: reactor development, uranium and heavy water production, and uranium isotope separation. In January 1942 the military decided fission would not contribute significantly to the war. The Heereswaffenamt handed the program to the Reich Research Council but kept funding it.
science.source_title: German nuclear program during World War II

science.text: A small team at the Henschel Flugzeugwerke, led by Herbert Wagner, searched for alternative energy sources for airplanes. It became interested in nuclear energy in 1940. Its application to found an Institute for Nuclear Technology and Nuclear Chemistry failed.
science.source_title: German nuclear program during World War II

science.text: Nazi leaders mainly encouraged science that gave obvious results and did not understand the significance of fundamental science. After the victory over France in 1940, Hitler decreed that military technical projects that could not be completed by 1942 should be cancelled.
science.source_title: Science and technology in Nazi Germany

science.text: Hugo Watzlawek wrote a detailed textbook on technical nuclear physics, recommending combined isotope separation methods to get enough enriched uranium. Walther Gerlach refused to print it, but the typed manuscript survived. It appeared in 1948 virtually unchanged, with a few additions on the 1945 US atomic bomb.
science.source_title: German nuclear program during World War II

politics.text: The Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations of 132 billion gold marks on Germany and limited its army to 100,000 men. It also banned conscription, armored vehicles, submarines and aircraft. The resulting economic devastation and public humiliation are considered leading factors in the rise of Adolf Hitler and Nazism.

On 9 November 1918, the Social Democrat Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a Republic in Germany. The Kaiser and all German ruling princes had abdicated amid internal revolution and a stalemated war. Two days later the new government received an armistice, which in practice was a surrender.
politics.source_title: History of Germany during World War I

politics.text: On 11 November 1918, Charles I of Austria, the last Habsburg ruler, issued a proclamation renouncing any role in state affairs. He issued a separate proclamation for Hungary two days later. Although he never officially abdicated, this is considered the end of the Habsburg dynasty.

The German Revolution of 1918-19 began at the end of October 1918 in Kiel, in northern Germany. Sailors mutinied at the prospect of a final battle against the British Navy. Through workers' and soldiers' councils, they quickly spread the revolt across Germany.
politics.source_title: History of Germany during World War I

politics.text: In 1919 the new republican Austrian government passed a law banishing the Habsburgs from Austrian territory until they renounced any intention of regaining the throne. In 1921 the Hungarian government dethroned the Habsburgs after Charles made attempts to regain the Hungarian throne. Hungary nonetheless remained a kingdom without a king until 1946.

The black-white-red flag was officially adopted as the national flag of the German Empire only in 1892, under Wilhelm II. In March 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg reinstated it by decree after the Nazi electoral victory. In September 1935 the swastika flag became the national flag, and the old imperial flag was banned as "reactionary".
Otto von Habsburg, the eldest son of Charles I, renounced all claims to the throne on 31 May 1961. Until then, the Habsburgs had not formally abandoned all hope of returning to power.

After the war, Germany's colonies were confiscated under the Treaty of Versailles and became League of Nations mandates. Yet talk of regaining them persisted until 1943. Konrad Adenauer, then mayor of Cologne, was among those calling for their return in the early Weimar Republic.

Historian Fritz Fischer argued in the 1960s that Germany had long desired to dominate Europe politically and economically. In his view, it seized the opportunity that opened in July 1914 and was guilty of starting the war. Other historians see the war as inadvertent, caused by complex accidents that overburdened the alliance system.
politics.source_title: German entry into World War I

politics.text: In 1925, Johannes Bell, who had been Colonial Minister in the Scheidemann cabinet, founded the Interparty Colonial Union. It included members of the whole political spectrum, from the Nazi party to the SPD. It aimed to recover Germany's lost colonies.

philosophy.text: Heidegger and Wittgenstein are considered two of the most influential philosophers of the 20th century. German-language philosophy fed both major modern traditions: analytic philosophy through figures like Frege and Wittgenstein, and continental phenomenology and hermeneutics through Husserl and Heidegger.

The Vienna Circle began as the Ernst Mach society. It formed to promote scientific thought and to combat the influence of Hegelian system-building, and it was led by Moritz Schlick. Schlick was murdered by his former student Johann Nelböck. The Nazis later expelled the Vienna Circle, entrenching it in American philosophy.

In 1946 the philosopher and psychologist Karl Jaspers gave lectures to students that were published as The Question of German Guilt. He argued that acknowledging national guilt was a necessary condition for the moral and political rebirth of Germany.

The Vienna Circle's philosophy, called logical positivism, was influenced by Wittgenstein. It held that everything meaningful is either an analytic truth or a verifiable synthetic truth, a strict test that set aside much traditional system-building.

In the 1960s and 1970s, Herbert Marcuse became known as the pre-eminent theorist of the New Left. Since the 1960s the Frankfurt School has been guided by Jürgen Habermas, whose work centers on communicative reason and linguistic intersubjectivity.

Jaspers believed that those who committed war crimes were morally guilty, and that those who tolerated them without resistance were politically guilty. He thought no one could escape collective guilt, and that taking responsibility might help Germans build a more morally responsible democracy.

Besides Schlick, the Vienna Circle included Philipp Frank, Rudolf Carnap, Hans Hahn and Otto Neurath. A closely related Berlin Circle was led by Hans Reichenbach and included Carl Hempel and the mathematician David Hilbert.

Martin Buber, described as an Austrian-Israeli existentialist, wrote I and Thou, published in 1923. He was influenced by Wilhelm Dilthey and Georg Simmel, two thinkers of the German school of Lebensphilosophie.

In 1945 the Swiss psychoanalyst Carl Jung wrote an influential essay treating collective guilt as a psychological phenomenon. He asserted that the German people felt a collective guilt (Kollektivschuld) for the atrocities committed by their fellow countrymen, and so introduced the term into German intellectual discourse. Jung said it was "for psychologists a fact" and that bringing the Germans to recognize this guilt would be one of the most important tasks of therapy. The same year, the theologian Martin Niemöller and other churchmen accepted shared guilt in the Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt.

German author and philosopher Bernhard Schlink says he sometimes feels that being German is a huge burden because of the country's past. He sees this guilt growing weaker from generation to generation.

culture.text: During the winter of 1916-17, a poor harvest left German cities short of potatoes, and people substituted almost inedible turnips, a vegetable usually fed to livestock. This 'Turnip Winter' was remembered with bitter distaste for generations. A British naval blockade had already caused severe food shortages, and the article says hundreds of thousands of civilians died from malnutrition, usually from typhus or another disease their weakened bodies could not resist.
culture.source_title: History of Germany during World War I

culture.text: In East Germany, Johann Sebastian Bach's birth on East German territory was celebrated by the government. It spent a great deal of money turning his house in Eisenach into a museum, which held more than 300 instruments from Bach's life. In 1980 the museum received more than 70,000 visitors.

Football is the most popular sport in Germany, and the German Football Association is the largest sports organisation of its kind worldwide, with more than 6,300,000 official members. The national team won the FIFA World Cup in 1954, 1974, 1990 and 2014.

Weimar culture was the burst of arts and sciences in Germany between its defeat in World War I in 1918 and Hitler's rise to power in 1933. Berlin in the 1920s was at its hectic center. Intellectuals, artists and innovators from many fields found it fertile ground.

East Germany hosted international schlager festivals. Rostock held one from 1962 to 1976, drawing participants from 18 to 22 countries each year. Dresden ran a similar festival from 1971 until shortly before reunification, and Magdeburg hosted a national contest from 1966 to 1971.

German films have won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film three times. Die Blechtrommel (The Tin Drum) won in 1979, Nowhere in Africa in 2002, and Das Leben der Anderen (The Lives of Others) in 2007.

Winter 1916-17 in Germany became known as the Turnip Winter. A Royal Navy blockade caused severe food shortages, and a poor harvest left the potato supply short, so Germans ate turnips, a vegetable usually fed to livestock, that were almost inedible. The meat ration in late 1916 was only 31% of peacetime levels and fell to 12% by late 1918. From August 1914 to mid-1919, about 474,000 civilians died in excess of peacetime from malnutrition, exhaustion, disease and despair.
culture.source_title: History of Germany during World War I

culture.text: In 1946, British occupation authorities in Hamburg issued eviction orders to make room for a new headquarters. In protest, 4,000 residents gathered, singing the outlawed Deutschlandlied and knocking the hats off fellow Hamburgers who kept their heads covered. The crowd chanted a variety of slogans, including "We're not Indians, not coolies, we must be treated like Germans", antisemitic slogans and "Gott strafe England". That last slogan led the Royal Military Police to arrest eleven members of the crowd.

Albert Einstein rose to public prominence during his years in Berlin and won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921. He was forced to flee Germany and the Nazi regime in 1933. German university faculties had become universally open to Jewish scholars in 1918.

East Germany's regime had an ambivalent attitude to jazz. It initially resisted it as an American influence on culture, but later accepted it as a form of 'people's music'. The Amiga record label began issuing American jazz recordings in 1963, and the singer Manfred Krug sang jazz until he emigrated in 1977.

Several East German rock stars left the GDR, where officials regulated rock music heavily, checking song texts for anti-state tendencies. Nina Hagen, who published her first hit Du hast den Farbfilm vergessen in 1974, emigrated in 1976. Veronika Fischer emigrated in 1981.

The number of Germans leaving their church peaked at a 'historical high' of 480,000 in 1939. The option to leave, called Kirchenaustritt, had existed since 1873, when Otto von Bismarck introduced it as part of the Kulturkampf against Catholicism. It was extended to Protestants for parity.

Ernst Lissauer coined the slogan Gott strafe England, which appeared on cufflinks and postcards in Germany. Helmut Herzfeld anglicised his name to John Heartfield in protest. Jaroslav Hašek mocked the phrase in his 1921 novel The Good Soldier Švejk, in which it labels a war liqueur.

East Germany introduced color television on the DFF2 channel in 1968, and the transition to color was completed in 1980. After the fall of the Iron Curtain, the state stations were gradually merged into the Federal Republic's public broadcasting system.
